header .subtitle: More options can mean fewer decisions. The research behind choice overload — and the patterns that get people past decision paralysis.
.law-origin .body-text: Barry Schwartz is an American psychologist who spent his career at Swarthmore College studying the intersection of psychology and economics. His 2004 book The Paradox of Choice argued that beyond a modest threshold, adding options makes people less satisfied, not more.

Trained at NYU and the University of Pennsylvania, Schwartz spent four decades teaching psychology at Swarthmore. His TED talk on the paradox became one of the most-watched ever, and his later work explored how defaults, satisficing, and ‘good enough’ choices protect people from decision fatigue.
.law-content .law-desc: Hick’s Law tells you a decision gets slower. The paradox of choice tells you it can fail to happen at all. Once a set crosses a threshold (the number varies with the task), users feel overwhelmed, defer, and convert less.

In practice
.card .desc: Sheena Iyengar’s 1995 supermarket experiment, published in 2000: a tasting display with 24 jams attracted more shoppers, but a display with only 6 jams converted ten times as many of the shoppers who stopped (30% versus 3%). More choice drew the crowd; less choice closed the sale.

When the cognitive cost of choosing exceeds the perceived benefit, users defer the decision entirely. They close the tab, save the cart for later, or pick “I’ll think about it” — and most never come back.
Users who finally choose from a large set are less satisfied than those who chose from a small one. Every alternative becomes a hypothetical regret — “what if I’d picked the other one?”
Editorial pre-selection — “our 5 picks” — converts better than the full catalog. The user trades infinite optionality for trust in your taste, and usually accepts.
How options are framed shapes which ones get picked. A pre-selected default, a recommended badge, or simply listing options in a particular order steers behavior more than the choice itself.
When you can’t reduce the catalog, let the user reduce it. Filters turn an unbrowsable 2,000 into a manageable 20 the user actually wants. Good filter UI is choice overload’s safety valve.

Use data — popularity, similar users, prior behavior — to pre-narrow the set. “Because you watched…” is a choice reduction in disguise, and it’s why streaming services don’t show their full catalog up front.
Side-by-side comparison is useful for 2–4 items. Past that, the table becomes a fresh source of overload — too many rows of subtle differences, no clear “best” answer.

No magic number — it depends on the decision’s stakes, the user’s expertise, and visual differentiation. But the field-tested range that avoids both arbitrary-feeling sparseness and overload is roughly 3 to 10, with most teams landing around 5 to 7.
Instead of 10,000 options, the model surfaces three good ones — or just does the task. Overload dissolves, replaced by a new question: do you trust the curation?
Letting AI choose removes decision fatigue but adds a trust cost. The best AI choices stay reversible and explain themselves, so the user keeps a sense of control.

.meta .value: Show fewer, recommend the right one
.ai-divider h3: The Paradox of Choice in the Age of AI
.ai-divider p: AI promises to cure overload by deciding for you — which trades the paralysis of too many options for the question of whether to trust the pick.
.apply-list li: You are designing a pricing page and the team wants to ship every plan variant the sales org has ever sold.
A catalog of 2,000 SKUs converts badly, and analytics show long sessions that end in abandoned carts rather than orders.
Onboarding asks new users to pick a template from forty options before they have any sense of what they need.
Cut any visible option set to the working range of 3 to 10, and group or filter whatever is left over.
Mark one option as recommended and pre-select it, so the default carries users who do not want to compare.
Cap side-by-side comparison at 4 items in the spec, and let users choose which 2 to put head to head.
